cmo-cmo-2018-01.prompt:
Consider an arrangement of tokens in the plane, not necessarily at distinct points. We are allowed to apply a sequence of moves of the following kind: select a pair of tokens at points $A$ and $B$ and move both of them to the midpoint of $A$ and $B$.

We say that an arrangement of $n$ tokens is *collapsible* if it is possible to end up with all $n$ tokens at the same point after a finite number of moves. Prove that every arrangement of $n$ tokens is collapsible if and only if $n$ is a power of $2$.
cmo-cmo-2018-01.answer: For $n = 2^k$ collapse two halves recursively and then pair them up; otherwise put $n-1$ tokens at $0$ and one at $1$ on a line: coordinates stay dyadic rationals, but the centroid $\frac1n$ (an invariant) is not dyadic.

cmo-cmo-2018-02.prompt: Let five points on a circle be labelled $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, and $E$ in clockwise order. Assume $AE = DE$ and let $P$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. Let $Q$ be the point on the line through $A$ and $B$ such that $A$ is between $B$ and $Q$ and $AQ = DP$. Similarly, let $R$ be the point on the line through $C$ and $D$ such that $D$ is between $C$ and $R$ and $DR = AP$. Prove that $PE$ is perpendicular to $QR$.
cmo-cmo-2018-02.answer: SAS congruences give $\triangle AQP \cong \triangle DPR$ (so $PQ = PR$) and $\triangle PAE \cong \triangle RDE$, $\triangle QAE \cong \triangle PDE$ (so $EQ = EP = ER$); hence $P$ and $E$ both lie on the perpendicular bisector of $QR$.

cmo-cmo-2018-03.prompt:
Two positive integers $a$ and $b$ are *prime-related* if $a = pb$ or $b = pa$ for some prime $p$. Find all positive integers $n$, such that $n$ has at least three divisors, and all the divisors can be arranged without repetition in a circle so that any two adjacent divisors are prime-related.

Note that $1$ and $n$ are included as divisors.
cmo-cmo-2018-03.answer: Exactly the $n$ that are neither a perfect square nor a power of a prime (i.e. $n$ has at least two distinct prime factors and some prime appears to an odd power).

cmo-cmo-2018-04.prompt:
Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients that have the following property: There exists a polynomial $q(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$p(1) + p(2) + p(3) + \cdots + p(n) = p(n)q(n)$$
for all positive integers $n$.
cmo-cmo-2018-04.answer: All constant polynomials, and $p(x) = c(x+r-1)(x+r-2)\cdots(x+r-d)$ with $c \ne 0$, $d \ge 1$ and $r \in \{0, 1, \dots, d\}$ (i.e. $p$ is a constant times a product of $d$ factors with consecutive integer roots, the roots including $0$ or $1$); then $q(x) = \frac{x+r}{d+1}$.

cmo-cmo-2018-05.prompt: Let $k$ be a given even positive integer. Sarah first picks a positive integer $N$ greater than $1$ and proceeds to alter it as follows: every minute, she chooses a prime divisor $p$ of the current value of $N$, and multiplies the current $N$ by $p^k - p^{-1}$ to produce the next value of $N$. Prove that there are infinitely many even positive integers $k$ such that, no matter what choices Sarah makes, her number $N$ will at some point be divisible by $2018$.
cmo-cmo-2018-05.answer: Take $k = 1009^j - 1$ ($j \ge 1$; $1009$ is prime). If $2018$ never divides $N$, the part $P$ of $N$ free of primes $\equiv 1 \pmod{1009}$ strictly decreases each minute, since every prime factor of $\frac{p^{k+1}-1}{p-1}$ is $\equiv 1 \pmod{1009}$ — impossible forever.
